Heat Generated in the System.
283.] The mechanical equivalent of the quantity of heat
generated in a conductor whose resistance is $R$ by a current $C$
in unit of time is, by Art. 242,
$$J H=R C^{2} .$$
(13)
We have therefore to determine the sum of such quantities as
$R C^{2}$ for all the conductors of the system.
For the conductor from $A_{p}$ to $A_{q}$ the conductivity is $K_{p q}$,
and the resistance $R_{p q}$, where
$$K_{p q} \cdot R_{p q}=1 .$$
(14)
The current in this conductor is, according to Obm's Law,
$$C_{p q}=K_{p q}\left(P_{p}-P_{q}\right) .$$
(15)
We shall suppose, however, that the value of the current is
not that given by Ohm's Law, but $X_{p q}$, where
$$X_{p q}=C_{p q}+Y_{p q} .$$
(16)
To determine the heat generated in the system we have to
find the sum of all the quantities of the form
$$\begin{gathered}
R_{p q} X^{2}{ }_{p q}, \\
\text { or } \quad J H=\Sigma\left\{R_{p q} G^{2}{ }_{p q}+2 R_{p q} C_{p q} Y_{p q}+R_{p q} Y^{2}{ }_{p q}\right\} .
\end{gathered}$$
(17)
Giving $C_{p q}$ its value, and remembering the relation between
$K_{p q}$ and $R_{p q}$, this becomes
$$\Sigma\left[\left(P_{p}-P_{q}\right)\left(C_{p q}+2 Y_{p q}\right)+R_{p q} Y^{2}{ }_{p q}\right] .$$
(18)

\section*{Heat Generated in the System.}

283.] The mechanical equivalent of the quantity of heat
 generated in a conductor whose resistance is $R$ by a current $C$
 in unit of time is, by Art. 242,

$$\begin{equation*}
J H=R C^{2} . \tag{13}
\end{equation*}$$


We have therefore to determine the sum of such quantities as
 $R C^{2}$ for all the conductors of the system.


For the conductor from $A_{p}$ to $A_{q}$ the conductivity is $K_{p q}$,
 and the resistance $R_{p q}$, where

$$\begin{equation*}
K_{p q} \cdot R_{p q}=1 . \tag{14}
\end{equation*}$$


The current in this conductor is, according to Obm's Law,

$$\begin{equation*}
C_{p q}=K_{p q}\left(P_{p}-P_{q}\right) . \tag{15}
\end{equation*}$$


We shall suppose, however, that the value of the current is
 not that given by Ohm's Law, but $X_{p q}$, where

$$\begin{equation*}
X_{p q}=C_{p q}+Y_{p q} . \tag{16}
\end{equation*}$$


To determine the heat generated in the system we have to
 find the sum of all the quantities of the form

$$\begin{gather*}
R_{p q} X^{2}{ }_{p q}, \\
\text { or } \quad J H=\Sigma\left\{R_{p q} G^{2}{ }_{p q}+2 R_{p q} C_{p q} Y_{p q}+R_{p q} Y^{2}{ }_{p q}\right\} .
\end{gather*}$$


Giving $C_{p q}$ its value, and remembering the relation between
 $K_{p q}$ and $R_{p q}$, this becomes

$$\begin{equation*}
\Sigma\left[\left(P_{p}-P_{q}\right)\left(C_{p q}+2 Y_{p q}\right)+R_{p q} Y^{2}{ }_{p q}\right] . \tag{18}
\end{equation*}$$
